<P class="p1159 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">71.17</SPAN><SPAN class="ft151">For example, an MNE Group has a Parent Entity (A Co) in Jurisdiction A which has two subsidiaries – B Co (in Jurisdiction B) and C Co (in Jurisdiction C). A Co is subject to CFC Tax Regimes at both the national level (National CFC Tax) and subnational level (Subnational CFC Tax). If the MNE Group made the </SPAN><NOBR>Five-Year</NOBR> Election with respect to Jurisdiction A, only current tax expense would be taken into account with respect to the National CFC Tax and Subnational CFC Tax. The deferred tax expenses or benefits with respect to these CFC Tax Regimes would be excluded from the Adjusted Covered Taxes of A Co, B Co and C Co. The <NOBR>Five-Year</NOBR> Election applies for all taxes for which there can be an allocation under Article 4.3.2(a), (c), (d) and (e) imposed on Constituent Entities located in Jurisdiction A. The MNE Group cannot elect to apply deferred tax expenses or benefits to National CFC Tax but not Subnational CFC Tax. Similarly, the election also cannot be made with respect to the allocation of CFC Taxes imposed on A Co with respect to CFCs in Jurisdiction B but not CFCs in Jurisdiction C.</P>
<P class="p1160 ft149">Allocation of deferred tax expenses and benefits from a Parent Entity to a Hybrid Entity or Reverse Hybrid Entity</P>
<P class="p1161 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">45.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The following paragraph will be inserted after paragraph 59.3 of the Commentary to Article 4.3.2(d):</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1162 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">59.4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft160">The principles outlined in paragraphs 71.4 to 71.17 of the Commentary to Article 4.4.1 also apply to the allocation of deferred taxes to a Hybrid Entity </SPAN><SPAN class="ft346">or </SPAN>Reverse Hybrid Entity under a tax transparency regime.</P>
<P class="p1163 ft149">Allocation of deferred tax expenses and benefits from a Main Entity to a Permanent Establishment</P>
<P class="p533 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">46.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The text in strikethrough will be deleted from paragraph 52 of the Commentary to Article 4.3.2(a):</SPAN></P>
<P class="p620 ft153"><SPAN class="ft119">52.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Determining the amount of Tax paid on a PE income inclusion is more complicated when </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft119">cross-crediting</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft119"> is allowed because Taxes paid by one PE are allowed to reduce the tax liability arising in respect of other PE income inclusions. </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft119">Cross-crediting</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft119"> means that the Tax paid with respect to an income inclusion from a </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft119">low-taxed</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft119"> PE may not equal the </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft119">pre-credit</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft119"> tax liability on the inclusion less the tax credit allowed for Taxes paid by that PE. </SPAN><SPAN class="ft347">Deferred tax liabilities with respect to PE income are allocated in the same manner. The rules with respect to the recognition of deferred tax liabilities are set forth in Article 4.4.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1164 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">47.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The following paragraph will be inserted after paragraph 52.34 of the Commentary to Article 4.3.2(a):</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1162 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">52.35.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft162">The principles outlined in paragraphs 71.4 to 71.13 and 71.16 to 71.17 of the Commentary to Article 4.4.1 also apply with respect to taxation regimes which include the income of foreign Permanent Establishments. With respect to such regimes, any taxes on GloBE Income which is Passive Income are allocated as part of step four as outlined in paragraphs 71.9 to 71.13. Paragraphs 71.14 and 71.15 are not applicable because the limitation in Article 4.3.3 is not applicable to the allocation of taxes on foreign Permanent Establishments under paragraph 4.3.2(a).</SPAN></P>
<P class="p574 ft149">Deferred tax expenses and benefits on Transition</P>
<P class="p533 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">48.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The text in bold will be added to paragraph 5 of the Commentary to Article 9.1.1:</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1165 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<P class="p799 ft153"><SPAN class="ft119">5.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">Article 9.1.1 sets out the deferred tax accounting attributes of a Constituent Entity that may be utilised in calculating the ETR in a jurisdiction in the Transition Year and subsequent years. Rather than requiring an MNE Group to undertake complex calculations as if the Constituent Entity had been subject to the GloBE Rules in prior years, it uses a simplified approach that allows the MNE Group to take into account the deferred tax accounting attributes of the MNE Group at the beginning of the Transition Year, at the lower of the Minimum Rate or the applicable domestic tax rate. The applicable domestic tax rate is the rate at which an item of deferred tax expense has been recorded in the financial accounts. However, deferred tax assets in respect of GloBE Losses that have been recorded at a rate lower than the Minimum Rate may be recast at the Minimum Rate if the taxpayer can demonstrate that the deferred tax asset is attributable to a loss that would have been a GloBE Loss had the MNE Group been subject to the GloBE Rules in the year in which the loss arose. These attributes include losses that have not been recognised due to an accounting recognition adjustment or valuation allowance. </SPAN>Any deferred tax assets or liabilities arising under a Blended CFC Tax Regime are disregarded for all jurisdictions for the purposes of Article 9.1.1.</P>
<P class="p807 ft148"><SPAN class="ft348">4.2.4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft349">Examples</SPAN></P>
<P class="p944 ft149">Example <NOBR>4.4.1(e)-3</NOBR></P>
<P class="p569 ft136"><SPAN class="ft128">1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft188">A Co is a Constituent Entity of a MNE Group in Country A. Country A imposes a 25% CIT rate and has a Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) Tax Regime which imposes Taxes on shareholders in respect of Passive Income derived by foreign (CFC) subsidiaries. Country A CFC Tax Regimes provides for the taxation of the CFC income by including such income in the domestic taxable income of the </SPAN><NOBR>CE-owner</NOBR> in the tax year immediately following the tax year when the income is derived by the CFC.</P>
<P class="p1166 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">A Co wholly owns B Co, which is located in Country B. Country B imposes a 5% CIT rate on Passive Income and imposes 9% CIT rate on operating income. B Co is the only Constituent Entity located in Country B.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p690 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">In year 1, B Co has GloBE Income of 200, of which 100 is Passive Income. B Co pays 14 of Country B tax, including 5 of Country B tax on Passive Income and 9 of Country B tax on other income.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">In Year 2, Country A imposes its CFC charge on the 100 of Passive Income earned by B Co in Year 1. This CFC charge is computed by applying the Country A CIT rate of 25% to the Passive Income earned by B Co, less any applicable foreign tax credit (FTC) for taxes paid on that Passive Income. In this context, A Co records a DTL for the deferred CFC tax </SPAN><NOBR>(pre-foreign</NOBR> tax credit) of 25 and records a DTA for the foreign tax credit of 5 for accounting purposes.</P>

<P class="p1173 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">7.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">Article 4.3.3 is then applied to limit the extent to which the deferred tax expense or benefit can be allocated to the CFC. <P class="p1184 ft136"><SPAN class="ft119">13.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft147">Before applying Article 4.3.3, it is necessary to calculate the allocations which would have been made in the absence of Article 4.3.3. First, there has been a reversal of previously allocated deferred tax expense (that is, </SPAN><NOBR>-2</NOBR> to A Co and <NOBR>-8</NOBR> to B Co). Second, the current taxes must be allocated. In this case, 20 of tax has been paid by A Co, all of which is allocable to B Co. This allocation is determined independently of the allocation of deferred taxes. Third, there is the allocation of further deferred tax expenses. In this case, there would be an allocation of 20 to B Co (this is the 50 in <NOBR>pre-foreign</NOBR> tax credit liability, recast to</P>
<P class="p1185 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">30</SPAN><SPAN class="ft130">and then subtracting the expected foreign tax credits of 10). As a result, prior to the application of Article 4.3.3, there would be a net allocation to B Co of 32 </SPAN><NOBR>(-8</NOBR> + 20 + 20).</P>
<P class="p1186 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">14.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Second, it is necessary to calculate the limitation under Article 4.3.3. Under Article 4.3.3, the ETR for Country B (ignoring any CFC Tax Regimes and tax transparency regimes) would have been 6.33% (=19/300). Its </SPAN><NOBR>Top-up</NOBR> Tax Percentage absent the application of CFC Tax Regimes and tax transparency regimes would be 8.67% <NOBR>(=15%-6.33%).</NOBR> Therefore, the maximum amount of CFC Taxes that can be allocated from Country A to Country B is 17.34 (the lesser of 32 and 17.34 (=8.67%×200)).</P>
<P class="p705 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">15.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">As the Article 4.3.3 limitation is less than the full allocation under the CFC Tax Regime, it is necessary to determine which amounts are not allocated due to the limitation. As outlined in paragraph 71.12, the allocations are made in the order (i) reversal of previously allocated amounts </SPAN><NOBR>(-8),</NOBR> (ii) current tax expenses (20) and (iii) further deferred tax expense (20). As <NOBR>-8</NOBR> is less than 17.34, the first allocation from the reversal of previously allocated amounts can be made. The second (ii) allocation can also be made as 12 <NOBR>(-8</NOBR> + 20) is less than 17.34. However, the final allocation cannot be made in full as 32 <NOBR>(-8</NOBR> +</P>
<P class="p701 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">20</SPAN><SPAN class="ft224">+ 20) is greater than 17.34. Accordingly, the full allocations are made under (i) and (ii) but only 5.34 (17.34 – 12) of (iii) can be allocated. Accordingly, of the 20 in further deferred tax expense, 5.34 is allocated to B Co and 14.66 (20 – 5.34) is retained by A Co due to the limitation in Article 4.3.3.</SPAN></P>

<P class="p737 ft136"><SPAN class="ft128">7.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft188">In year 1, A Co records a DTL of 120 based on the timing difference of the machine in the PE. The DTL on the PE income of 120 is recast to 90 (recasting from a 20% rate to a 15% rate) and the creditable foreign taxes with respect to this amount remains 15 (it is not recast). Accordingly, the net deferred tax</SPAN></P>
<P class="p596 ft119">expense allocable to PE is 75 = <NOBR>(90-15).</NOBR> The deferred tax expense for purposes of calculating Adjusted Covered Taxes in PE is 90 (=15+75). This is the PE’s own deferred tax expense of 15 in addition to the allocation of 75 in deferred tax expense allocated from A Co. The deferred tax expense of 105 accrued by A Co shall not be included in the Adjusted Covered Taxes of A Co for GloBE purposes.</P>

<P class="p1200 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p513 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p514 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p1145 ft112"><SPAN class="ft24">| </SPAN>111</P>
<P class="p1201 ft140"><SPAN class="ft139">5.</SPAN> Allocation of profits and taxes in</P>
<P class="p1202 ft359">structures including <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities</P>
<P class="p1203 ft131">5.1. Introduction</P>
<P class="p541 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">The GloBE Rules are designed to ensure that multinational enterprises pay a minimum level of tax on their profits in each jurisdiction. There are consequently rules to determine how profits and taxes should be allocated between jurisdictions.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">This guidance clarifies how the rules are intended to allocate profits and taxes between Constituent Entities in structures where different jurisdictions take different views as to whether Entities in the structure are fiscally transparent. This guidance is important to ensure profits and taxes are allocated appropriately and consistently between jurisdictions.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">Generally, the GloBE Rules assign profits to the Constituent Entity that earned the income. The jurisdiction where that Constituent Entity is located would typically have, or be expected to have, the right to tax those profits. So, for example, the GloBE Rules assign profits of a Permanent Establishment to the Permanent Establishment and those profits are reflected in the GloBE computations of the jurisdiction where the Permanent Establishment is located. Similarly, Article 3.2.3 generally requires adjustments to ensure that the allocation of profits between Constituent Entities reflects the allocation of profit between those entities for local tax purposes. These income allocation rules are designed to ensure that the Effective Tax Rate computation for each jurisdiction appropriately reflects the existing allocation of taxing rights between jurisdictions.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p564 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft138">The income allocation rules are complemented by Article 4.3, which reallocates Covered Taxes between Constituent Entities. The Article applies to specified cases when a Constituent Entity is charged tax in respect of the profits of another Constituent Entity. It reallocates that tax to the Constituent Entity that recognises the profit under the GloBE Rules. This ensures that the ETR calculation in each jurisdiction properly reflects the full amount of taxes that the multinational has paid on those profits. The tax is matched with the income that has been subject to the tax.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p557 ft144"><SPAN class="ft128">5.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft143">The principle of matching the tax with the income that has been subject to the tax also applies to </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities (i.e. entities that are fiscally transparent in the jurisdiction where the entity is created). However, instead of moving the tax to the location of the income as in the case of taxes on the income of a Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) or Permanent Establishment, profit of a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is assigned to the Constituent Entity that is, or would be expected to be, taxable on those profits. Article 3.5.1 sets out how this profit should be allocated. Under this article, the profit is first allocated to any Permanent Establishment through which the business of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is carried on. This means the profits will be attributed to the jurisdiction where the profit was earned (which will often be the jurisdiction where the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity was created) when that jurisdiction has taxing rights over those business profits.</P>
<P class="p608 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">219</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_220">


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p11 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p485 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p521 ft24"><SPAN class="ft153">112</SPAN><SPAN class="ft118">|</SPAN></P>
<P class="p522 ft119">Any profits that are not allocated to a Permanent Establishment are then allocated to its owners to the extent that the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is treated as fiscally transparent in the jurisdiction of the owner, i.e. it is a Tax Transparent Entity. Thus, the profits are allocated to the owner under the GloBE Rules if the owner is taxed on its share of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity’s profits. This treatment is designed to match the income with the tax on a jurisdictional basis.</P>
<P class="p525 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">6.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">If, on the other hand, the </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is not treated as fiscally transparent in the jurisdiction of an owner, i.e. it is a Reverse Hybrid Entity, that owner’s share of the profits is not allocated and remains the profits of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity, which is treated as a Stateless Entity. This reflects that the MNE Group is not subject to <NOBR>residence-based</NOBR> taxation on those profits in either the jurisdiction where the Flow- through Entity was created or the jurisdiction of its owner.</P>
<P class="p546 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">7.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">This Administrative Guidance considers various issues relating to the allocation of profits under Article 3.5.1(b) as well as related issues with the profit and tax allocation of </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities and Hybrid Entities. However, the Administrative Guidance does not address issues relating to Permanent Establishments and so the issues discussed, and examples cited, assume either that there is no Permanent Establishment through which the business of a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is carried on, or that the allocation under Article 3.5.1(a) has already occurred prior to the allocation of the remaining profits of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity.</P>
<P class="p524 ft131"><SPAN class="ft131">5.2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft222">Application of Article 3.5.1(b) and Article 10.2.1 definitions</SPAN></P>
<P class="p521 ft148">5.2.1. Issue 1: Tax law of the jurisdiction in which the owner is located</P>
<P class="p603 ft142"><SPAN class="ft119">8.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft141">Article 10.2.1 determines whether a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is classified as a Tax Transparent Entity or a Reverse Hybrid Entity based on how the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is treated in the “jurisdiction in which the owner is located”. This determination is made with respect to each Ownership Interest so a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity can be both a Tax Transparent Entity and a Reverse Hybrid Entity where it has multiple owners.</P>
<P class="p576 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">9.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">Paragraph 154 of the Commentary to Article 10.2.1 of the Model Rules states that the reference to the “jurisdiction in which the owner is located” refers to the jurisdiction of the direct owner of the Flow- through Entity. Accordingly, the difference between a Tax Transparent Entity and a Reverse Hybrid Entity depends on whether the domestic tax law of the jurisdiction of the direct owner treats the Entity as fiscally transparent.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p694 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">10.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Stakeholders have identified that there is some uncertainty over how Article 10.2.1 applies when a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is held directly by another <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity.</P>
<P class="p525 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">11.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The uncertainty arises because </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities are generally treated as Stateless Constituent Entities that do not have a location under the GloBE Rules. Some have interpreted this to mean that a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity cannot be the direct owner for the purposes of Article 10.2.1 because it is not located in a jurisdiction (unless it is the UPE or an Intermediate Parent Entity that is subject to an IIR). Under this interpretation, the direct owner would consequently be ignored, and Article 10.2.1 would be applied by reference to the next owner further up the ownership chain.</P>
<P class="p851 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">12.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">In contrast, others have interpreted that the direct owner of the </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is the owner for the purposes of Article 10.2.1, even if that direct owner is a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity.</P>
<P class="p525 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">13.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">These different interpretations could result in implementing jurisdictions attributing profits to different jurisdictions, creating a significant risk of uncoordinated outcomes and multiple jurisdictions imposing </SPAN><NOBR>top-up</NOBR> taxes in relation to the same profits.</P>
<P class="p797 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">14.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This is illustrated in the following example.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p717 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>

</DIV>

<DIV id="id_1">

<P class="p514 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p1145 ft112"><SPAN class="ft24">| </SPAN>113</P>
<P class="p1204 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">15.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This example is based on a structure where A Co wholly owns B Co and B Co owns C Co. A Co is located in Jurisdiction A. B Co and C Co were created in Jurisdictions B and C respectively but are fiscally transparent in those jurisdictions and are thus treated as Stateless Constituent Entities under the</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1125 ft119">GloBE Rules. B Co has 100 of profit and C Co has 200 of profit. The table below summarises how each jurisdiction’s tax laws treat the Entities.</P>
<P class="p1205 ft128">Classification of Entities in the ownership chain</P>
<TABLE cellpadding=0 cellspacing=0 class="t83">
<TR>
	<TD class="tr13 td654"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr13 td655"><P class="p78 ft128">Jurisdiction</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr13 td655"><P class="p1206 ft128">A Co</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr13 td656"><P class="p1206 ft128">B Co</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr13 td657"><P class="p75 ft128">C Co</P></TD>
</TR>
<TR>
	<TD class="tr33 td658"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr33 td659"><P class="p78 ft128">A</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr33 td659"><P class="p1207 ft128">Opaque</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr33 td660"><P class="p1208 ft310">Transparent</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr33 td661"><P class="p75 ft128">Opaque</P></TD>
</TR>
<TR>
	<TD class="tr13 td161"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td662"><P class="p78 ft128">B</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td663"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td660"><P class="p1208 ft310">Transparent</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td661"><P class="p1209 ft310">Transparent</P></TD>
</TR>
<TR>
	<TD class="tr31 td512"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td664"><P class="p78 ft128">C</P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td665"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td666"><P class="p13 ft127"> </P></TD>
	<TD class="tr31 td667"><P class="p75 ft128">Transparent</P></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
<P class="p1068 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">16.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">In this case, the tax base of A Co would include B Co’s profit of 100. It will not include C Co’s profit of 200 because under jurisdiction A’s law, C Co is not fiscally transparent.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p555 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">17.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The profits of C Co will also not be taxable in Jurisdictions B or C. This is because both B Co and C Co are considered fiscally transparent in the jurisdiction in which they are created and are consequently not subject to Covered Taxes in respect of their income.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">18.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Under the GloBE Rules, the 100 profit of B Co will be allocated to A Co. This is because B Co is a Tax Transparent Entity in relation to A Co. However, the allocation of the 200 profit of C Co depends upon whether Jurisdiction A or Jurisdiction B is considered the jurisdiction where the “owner” is located for the purposes of Article 10.2.1(a) and (b).</SPAN></P>
<P class="p762 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">19.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft154">If Jurisdiction A were considered the jurisdiction of the owner under Article 10.2.1, C Co would be</SPAN></P>
<P class="p855 ft119">treated as a Reverse Hybrid Entity because Jurisdiction A views C Co as fiscally opaque. This would result in C Co’s 200 of profits being attributed to C Co and included in a separate ETR computation.</P>
<P class="p553 ft136"><SPAN class="ft119">20.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft147">Alternatively, if Jurisdiction B were considered the jurisdiction of the owner, then C Co would be treated as a Tax Transparent Entity because Jurisdiction B views C Co as fiscally transparent. C Co’s 200 of profits would be allocated to A Co because B Co is also a Tax Transparent Entity. Under this analysis, A Co’s adjusted profits would be 300, despite the fact A Co is only subject to tax on 100 of those profits.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1210 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<DIV id="page_222">


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p11 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p485 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p521 ft24"><SPAN class="ft153">114</SPAN><SPAN class="ft118">|</SPAN></P>
<P class="p522 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">21.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This question of which owner is relevant for purposes of Article 10.2.1 needs to be clarified in order to prevent uncoordinated application of the rules. The Inclusive Framework considers that the status of a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity as a Tax Transparent Entity or Reverse Hybrid Entity should generally be determined by reference to the tax law of the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> closest to such Entity in the ownership chain that is not itself a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity.</P>
<P class="p589 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">22.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This interpretation of “owner” is more consistent with the underlying principles of profit allocation and matching taxes with the related income that are reflected in the GloBE Rules. Under these principles, the profits of a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity should only be allocated to an owner when the owner is subject to tax on those profits, in order to ensure that the income and the tax with respect to that income are included in the same jurisdictional ETR computation. Conversely, if an owner is not subject to tax on the income, the profits should remain with the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity.</P>
<P class="p1053 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">23.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">It follows from this that the profits of a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity should not generally be allocated to another <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity (a <NOBR>‘Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner’) under the GloBE Rules. This is because the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner will typically not be subject to a Covered Tax on its profits or the profits of an Entity that it owns, given it is treated as fiscally transparent under the tax laws of the jurisdiction in which it was created.</P>
<P class="p525 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">24.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This will be true for both stateless </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities and <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities which are located in a jurisdiction because they are required to apply the IIR. In both cases, the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner will not be subject to a Covered Tax on its profits or the profits of an Entity that it owns. Consequently, the profits should not be allocated to a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner in either case and the application of Article 10.2.1 will not depend upon the location of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner.</P>
<P class="p546 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">25.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">There is however an exception when the </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner is the UPE of the MNE Group <NOBR>(‘Flow-through</NOBR> UPE'). This is because the owners of the UPE will not be Constituent Entities of the MNE Group. As such, the profits of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity owner or any <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities it owns cannot be allocated to these owners. The owners could nonetheless be subject to tax on those profits. Article 7.1 is designed to address this situation by reducing the GloBE Income of the UPE to the extent that the owners are subject to tax on those profits (or the other conditions in Article 7.1 are met). The profits of a Flow- through Entity will be allocated to the UPE so that Article 7.1 is tested by reference to the total profits that could be subject to tax in the hands of the owners.</P>
<P class="p546 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">26.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Consequently, the Commentary will be updated to clarify that a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity (other than a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE) will not be considered an owner for the purposes of Article 10.2.1. Instead, the owner for the purposes of Article 10.2.1 will be the next owner further up the ownership chain that is not a Flow- through Entity or where there is no such Entity, a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE (referred to as the Reference Entity in the guidance below).</P>
<P class="p547 ft142"><SPAN class="ft119">27.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft152">This means that the treatment of an Entity as a Tax Transparent Entity or Reverse Hybrid Entity will depend on how the tax law of the Reference Entity’s jurisdiction treats the Entity. Further, because this determination is made based on each Ownership Interest, an Entity with multiple owners in different</SPAN></P>
<P class="p739 ft136">jurisdictions could have more than one classification for GloBE purposes. Where this guidance refers to the tax law of the relevant Entity’s jurisdiction, it is referring to all of the laws of the jurisdiction that result in treatment of the Entity as fiscally transparent and taxation of its income or loss at the owner level. In</P>
<P class="p548 ft119">other words, tax law in the context of determining whether an Entity is fiscally transparent means the jurisdiction’s laws, including tax laws, that affirmatively provide for the result that the Entity’s income, expenditure, profit or loss is considered that of the owner for purposes of a Covered Tax.</P>
<P class="p1211 ft142"><SPAN class="ft119">28.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft152">The Commentary will also be updated to clarify what is meant by fiscally transparent in the case of an Entity that is not subject to a corporate income tax or other Covered Tax. A jurisdiction must have tax laws that affirmatively provide for fiscal transparent treatment to satisfy the definition. Accordingly, a jurisdiction that does not have a generally applicable corporate income tax or a similar Covered Tax cannot</SPAN></P>
<P class="p592 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<P class="p539 ft119">be considered to treat an Entity created in the jurisdiction or an Entity owned by an Entity created in the jurisdiction as fiscally transparent. However, an Entity located in a jurisdiction without a corporate income tax may still be considered a Tax Transparent Entity in certain cases under Article 10.2.4.</P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">29.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This rule also appropriately addresses situations where more than one owner is subject to tax on a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity’s income. This can arise when an owner that is subject to tax on the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity’s income is a Hybrid Entity. This is illustrated in the following example.</P>

<P class="p744 ft136"><SPAN class="ft119">30.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft147">The example is the same as that in paragraphs 14 and 15 above, except that C Co is viewed as fiscally transparent in Jurisdiction A and not fiscally transparent in Jurisdiction B; and there is a fourth Entity at the top of the structure, Hold Co. The tax laws of Hold Co’s jurisdiction treat the three other Entities in the ownership chain as fiscally transparent. Both Hold Co and A Co are subject to tax on C Co’s income. This raises the question which Entity should be allocated C Co’s profit under the GloBE Rules.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p735 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">31.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This guidance allocates C Co’s profit to A Co because it is the Entity closest to C Co in the ownership chain that is not a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity, i.e. it is not fiscally transparent in its jurisdiction. A Co meets the definition of a Hybrid Entity because Jurisdiction Z views A Co as fiscally transparent. Consequently, any taxes that Hold Co pays on C Co’s profits will be reallocated to A Co under Article 4.3.2(d).</P>
<P class="p792 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<P class="p522 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">32.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This solution ensures that the principle of matching the tax with the income that has been subject to the tax is satisfied. C Co’s profits and taxes on those profits will be recognised in the same jurisdictional ETR computation. The solution is consistent with the general approach to the profit and tax allocation of Hybrid Entities, which is to recognise the profit in the Hybrid Entity and then allocate any taxes in respect of these profits paid by the owner to the Hybrid Entity.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p521 ft148">5.2.2. Guidance</P>
<P class="p1217 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">33.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The strikethrough text will be deleted, and the bold text will be added to paragraphs 154 to 156 of the Commentary to Article 10.2.1.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1218 ft153"><SPAN class="ft119">154.</SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft202">Flow-through</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft119"> Entities can further be divided into two categories: Tax Transparent Entities and Reverse Hybrid Entities. The difference between these terms depends on how </SPAN>those Entities are treated under the tax law of <SPAN class="ft119">the </SPAN><SPAN class="ft211">direct</SPAN><SPAN class="ft119"> owners (i.e. </SPAN>direct or indirect <SPAN class="ft119">owners of their Ownership Interest) </SPAN><SPAN class="ft211">are treating them under their domestic tax law</SPAN><SPAN class="ft119">. </SPAN>The determination of whether a tested Entity is a Tax Transparent Entity or Reverse Hybrid Entity is made for each Ownership Interest. As a result, an Entity with multiple owners in different jurisdictions could have more than one classification for GloBE purposes.</P>
<P class="p1219 ft201">154.1 Whether a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity (the tested Entity) is a Tax Transparent Entity or a Reverse Hybrid Entity depends on how the tax law of the jurisdiction in which the Reference Entity is located treats the tested Entity and each Entity through which the Reference Entity owns its Ownership Interest in the tested Entity. The Reference Entity is the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> that is closest in the ownership chain to the tested Entity and that is either (a) not a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity or (b) where there is no such Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner,</NOBR> a Flow- through Entity that is the Ultimate Parent Entity of the MNE Group <NOBR>(Flow-through</NOBR> UPE).</P>
<P class="p1220 ft153"><SPAN class="ft119">155.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft202">A </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft119">Flow-through</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft119"> Entity is a Tax Transparent Entity if the tax law of the </SPAN>Reference Entity’s jurisdiction treats the tested Entity and each Entity through which the Reference Entity owns its Ownership Interest in the tested Entity <SPAN class="ft211">owners also treat it as fiscally transparent. and requires the owner to recognize the income, expenditure, profit or loss of the </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft211">Flow-through</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft211"> Entity as if it was income earned or expenditure borne by the owners</SPAN><SPAN class="ft119">.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1221 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">156.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft360">On the other hand, a A </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft211">Flow-through</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft211"> Entity is a Reverse Hybrid Entity if the domestic t</SPAN>ax law of the jurisdiction in which the Reference Entity is located does not treat the tested Entity and each Entity through which the Reference Entity owns its Ownership Interest in the tested Entity <SPAN class="ft211">the owners are not treating it as fiscally transparent and therefore, it does not recognize the income, expenditure, profit or loss when earned or incurred by the Entity, but until the Entity distributes profits or make an equivalent payment to its owners</SPAN>.</P>
<P class="p611 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">34.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The bold text will be added to paragraph 160 of the Commentary to Article 10.2.2.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p617 ft142"><SPAN class="ft119">160.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft268">Article 10.2.2 describes what is meant by fiscally transparent in Articles 10.2.1 and 10.2.5. It states that an Entity is treated as fiscally transparent under the laws of a jurisdiction, if such jurisdiction treats the income, expenditure, profit or loss of that Entity as if they were derived or</SPAN></P>
<P class="p803 ft210"><SPAN class="ft212">incurred by the direct owner of the Entity in proportion to its interest. </SPAN>This requires the jurisdiction to have laws that affirmatively provide for the result that the Entity’s income, expenditure, profit or loss is considered to be the owner’s income, expenditure, profit or loss for purposes of a Covered Tax. For example, a jurisdiction that does not have a corporate income tax or a similar Covered Tax cannot be considered to treat an Entity created in the jurisdiction or an Entity owned by an Entity created in the jurisdiction as fiscally transparent.</P>
<P class="p1222 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<P class="p593 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">35.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The strikethrough text in the heading will be deleted, and paragraph 214 to the Commentary to Article 3.5.1 is replaced by a new paragraph 214.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p645 ft119">Residual allocated to <SPAN class="ft211">direct</SPAN> owners</P>
<P class="p643 ft211"><SPAN class="ft211">214.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft360">If the Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owners</NOBR> are also Tax Transparent Entities, then paragraph (b) of Article 3.5.1 applies again and allocates the residual Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss to the next Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> up the ownership chain (unless the Ownership Interest holder is</P>
<P class="p658 ft211">the UPE, in which case Article 3.5.1(c) applies). Thus, if all the Constituent Entities are Tax Transparent Entities (i.e. a Tax Transparent Structure), all of the MNE Group’s income or loss is ultimately allocated to the UPE under Article 3.5.1(b) and 3.5.1(c).</P>
<P class="p626 ft153"><SPAN class="ft119">214.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft361">The income of a Tax Transparent Entity is allocated to the Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> that is the Reference Entity under Article 10.2.1. This ensures the income allocation is consistent with the rules that classify a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity as a Tax Transparent Entity or Reverse Hybrid Entity.</P>
<P class="p807 ft148"><SPAN class="ft348">5.2.3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft349">Examples</SPAN></P>
<P class="p595 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">36.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft154">The following examples will be included in the GloBE Model Rules Examples.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p624 ft149">Example <NOBR>10.2.1-1</NOBR></P>
<P class="p625 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">Assume Hold Co owns A Co, A Co owns B Co, and B Co owns C Co. Hold Co is not a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. The tax law of the jurisdiction in which Hold Co is located, Jurisdiction Z, treats Hold Co as a fiscally opaque entity and A Co, B Co and C Co as fiscally transparent. The tax law of the jurisdiction in which A Co is located, Jurisdiction A, treats A Co as fiscally opaque, and B Co and C Co as fiscally transparent. The tax law of the jurisdiction in which B Co is created, Jurisdiction B, treats B Co as fiscally transparent but treats C Co as fiscally opaque. The tax law of the jurisdiction in which C Co is created, Jurisdiction C, treats C Co as fiscally transparent. See illustration below.</P>

<P class="p618 ft119">of the jurisdiction where it was created (Jurisdiction C). It is a Tax Transparent Entity because A Co is the Reference Entity and Jurisdiction A’s tax laws treat C Co and every Constituent Entity through which A Co’s Ownership Interest in C Co is owned as fiscally transparent. A Co is the Reference Entity because it is the closest Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> to C Co that is not treated as fiscally transparent under the tax laws in its place of creation (i.e. a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity).</P>
<P class="p638 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft362">In accordance with Article 3.5.1(b), the profit or loss of C Co is consequently allocated to A Co</SPAN></P>
<P class="p806 ft119">because A Co is the Reference Entity which determined that C Co is a Tax Transparent Entity. A Co also meets the Hybrid Entity definition because Jurisdiction Z’s tax laws treat A Co as fiscally transparent so A Co’s profits are subject to tax in both Jurisdiction A and Jurisdiction Z. Consequently, any Covered Taxes paid by Hold Co with respect to C Co’s income shall be allocated to A Co under Article 4.3.2(d) because A Co is a Hybrid Entity and the profit or loss of C Co has been allocated to A Co.</P>

The tax law of the jurisdiction in which B Co is created, Jurisdiction B, treats B Co and C Co as fiscally transparent. The tax law of the jurisdiction in which C Co is created treats C Co as fiscally transparent. Assume B Co’s profit is</P>

C Co’s profit is consequently allocated to C Co under Article 3.5.1(c).</P>
<P class="p1233 ft131"><SPAN class="ft131">5.3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft222">Application of Article 3.5.3</SPAN></P>
<P class="p537 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">37.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Article 3.5.3 reduces a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity’s Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss by the amount of income or loss that is allocable to owners that are not Group Entities and whose Ownership Interests in the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity are owned directly or indirectly through a Tax Transparent Structure. This ensures that the MNE Group does not pay <NOBR>top-up</NOBR> tax on income that it is not entitled to and on which no Constituent Entity is subject to tax.</P>
<P class="p1053 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">38.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Two issues have been raised around the application of this Article. The first concerns the application of Article 3.5.3 to a partially owned </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity when the UPE of the MNE Group is also a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. The second concerns how Article 3.5.3 applies when the minority owners hold their interest in the tested Entity indirectly through another Constituent Entity of the MNE Group.</P>
<P class="p521 ft148">5.3.1. Issue 2a: Interaction of Article 3.5.3 and Article 3.5.4(b)</P>
<P class="p537 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">39.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Article 3.5.4 states that Article 3.5.3 does not apply in the following two scenarios: (a) where the UPE of the MNE Group is a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity; and (b) where such a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE owns the Flow- through Entity directly or indirectly through a Tax Transparent Structure.</P>
<P class="p546 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">40.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Article 3.5.4 was included to ensure that Ownership Interests that </SPAN><NOBR>non-group</NOBR> Entities hold in the UPE do not cause the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss of a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity to be reduced under Article 3.5.3. Otherwise, Article 3.5.3 could have resulted in the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss of a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity being reduced to zero where the UPE is the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity or where the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is owned by a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE through a Tax Transparent Structure. This is because the owners of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE are all <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities. This would essentially have excluded the Entity, and potentially the entire MNE Group, from the GloBE Rules irrespective of whether the income is taxed in the hands of the <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> owners. Instead, Article 7.1 applies and defines the conditions that needs to be met for the income to be reduced.</P>
<P class="p559 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">41.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Stakeholders have identified some uncertainty over how Article 3.5.4(b) applies to </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities that are not wholly owned by the UPE. Some have interpreted Article 3.5.4(b) to only disapply Article 3.5.3 with respect to Ownership Interests in the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity that are owned by <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities through the UPE. This would mean that the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss allocable to other <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities would still be excluded by Article 3.5.3. Others consider that Article 3.5.3 does not apply to any Ownership Interests owned by <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities when Article 3.5.4(b) is met. The impact of the different interpretations is illustrated in the following example.</P>
<P class="p1234 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<P class="p1235 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">42.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">In this example, A Co is the UPE of the MNE Group and a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. It is owned by Invest Co. A Co holds 80% of the Ownership Interests in B Co, a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity that is part of the same MNE Group. The remaining 20% of the Ownership Interests in B Co are directly held by persons that are not Group Entities. The Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss of B Co is 100.</P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">43.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Article 3.5.4 will apply because A Co is a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE. This ensures that B Co’s Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss is not reduced because of Invest Co’s Ownership Interests in A Co. The interpretation that Article 3.5.4 disapplies Article 3.5.3 fully would mean that none of the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss of B Co will be excluded. The full 100 would be allocated to A Co in accordance with Article 3.5.1(b). Because the owners of the UPE will not be subject to tax on the 20 of income that is attributable to the Ownership Interests in B Co owned by <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities, it is unlikely the GloBE Income of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> UPE would be reduced to nil under Article 7.1. This could result in the MNE Group paying a <NOBR>top-up</NOBR> tax liability in respect of the income attributable to the <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entity owners. This would be inconsistent with the policy intention of Articles 3.5.3 and 3.5.4.</P>
<P class="p555 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">44.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Alternatively, if Article 3.5.4(b) applies to the extent that the Ownership Interests are owned directly or indirectly by the UPE, then it means that Article 3.5.3 continues to apply with respect to the Ownership Interests owned by </SPAN><NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities. The effect is that the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss of B Co is reduced by 20 in accordance with Article 3.5.3 and the remaining 80 are then allocated to A Co in accordance with Article 3.5.1(b).</P>
<P class="p564 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">45.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This provides for the correct answer on the application of Article 3.5.3 because the provision continues to apply to Ownership Interests owned by persons that are not Group Entities and not the UPE. It also provides for a consistent answer because it has the same effect on:</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1236 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">a.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft155">a structure where the Ownership Interests in the </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity are owned directly by the UPE and directly or indirectly (through a Tax Transparent Structure) by persons that are not Group Entities; and</P>
<P class="p1237 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>

<DIV id="id_1">

<P class="p485 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p521 ft24"><SPAN class="ft153">122</SPAN><SPAN class="ft118">|</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1238 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">b.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft155">a structure where the Ownership Interests are owned indirectly by the UPE through a Tax Transparent Structure, and directly or indirectly (through a Tax Transparent Structure) by persons that are not Group Entities.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p525 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">46.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Therefore, this guidance clarifies that Article 3.5.4(b) applies when the Ownership Interests in the </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity are owned by the UPE directly or indirectly through a Tax Transparent Structure and applies to the extent of the Ownership Interests owned by the UPE.</P>
<P class="p521 ft148">5.3.2. Guidance</P>
<P class="p750 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">47.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The bold text and new paragraph 232.1 will be added to the Commentary to Article 3.5.4:</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1218 ft119">232<SPAN class="ft153">. </SPAN>Article 3.5.4 sets out two cases where Article 3.5.3 does not apply. The first one is included in paragraph (a) which covers the case where the UPE is a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. <SPAN class="ft211">Paragraph (b) covers the situation where the </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft211">Flow-through</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft211"> Entity is held by a </SPAN><NOBR><SPAN class="ft211">Flow-through</SPAN></NOBR><SPAN class="ft211"> UPE </SPAN><SPAN class="ft347">directly or </SPAN><SPAN class="ft211">through a Tax Transparent Structure. These cases are</SPAN><SPAN class="ft153"> This case is </SPAN>not contemplated in Article 3.5.3 because all of the owners of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity are <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> owners, <SPAN class="ft211">which</SPAN><SPAN class="ft153"> and </SPAN>is <SPAN class="ft153">instead </SPAN>covered by Article 7.1.</P>
<P class="p617 ft201">232.1. Paragraph 3.5.4(b) disapplies Article 3.5.3 in relation to Ownership Interests of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity that are owned directly by the UPE or indirectly by the UPE through a</P>
<P class="p803 ft210">Tax Transparent Structure. This ensures the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss of a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is not reduced due to Ownership Interests of the UPE’s owner(s). Instead, Article 3.5.1 will apply to allocate the profit of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity between Constituent Entities, and Article 7.1 would apply to the UPE. However, Article 3.5.4(b) only disapplies Article 3.5.3 in respect of owners which have indirect Ownership Interests in the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity through Ownership Interests in the UPE. Article 3.5.3 will continue to apply to the extent that Ownership Interests in the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity are owned by non- Group Entities either directly or indirectly through Ownership Interests in Entities other than the UPE.</P>
<P class="p577 ft148">5.3.3. Example</P>
<P class="p750 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">48.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The following example will be included in the GloBE Model Rules Examples.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p572 ft149">Example <NOBR>3.5.4-1</NOBR></P>
<P class="p1239 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">A Co is the UPE of the MNE Group and a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. It owns 80% of the Ownership Interests in B Co, a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity that is part of the same MNE Group. The remaining 20% of the Ownership Interests in B Co are owned by persons that are not Group Entities.</P>
<P class="p617 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">The profit of B Co is 100. In this case, Article 3.5.4(b) applies only with respect to the 80% of the Ownership Interests in B Co that are owned by the UPE (which represent 80 of B Co’s profit). This means that Article 3.5.3 still applies with respect to the 20% of the Ownership Interests in B Co that are owned by the persons that are not Group Entities and therefore, B Co’s profit should be reduced by 20 prior to the allocation of the profit in accordance with Article 3.5.1.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1240 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">230</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_231">
<DIV id="p231dimg1">
<INGENBILD zsrc="HD0322231x1.jpg/" id="p231img1">
</DIV>


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p513 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p514 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p1145 ft112"><SPAN class="ft24">| </SPAN>123</P>
<P class="p1241 ft166"><SPAN class="ft348">5.3.4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft363">Issue 2b: Application of Article 3.5.3 when a minority owner holds its interest indirectly through another Constituent Entity</SPAN></P>
<P class="p710 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">49.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">As above, Article 3.5.3 reduces the FANIL of a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity by the amount that is allocable to owners that are not Group Entities (‘minority owners’). This reduction applies when these owners hold their interest in the tested Entity either directly or through a Tax Transparent Structure.</P>
<P class="p553 ft128"><SPAN class="ft119">50.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft146">Where a minority owner holds its Ownership Interests in the tested Entity directly, the FANIL of the tested Entity will be reduced under Article 3.5.3 regardless of whether the tax laws of the minority owner’s</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1126 ft119">jurisdiction treat the tested Entity as a fiscally transparent entity. The FANIL will consequently be reduced even in cases where the minority owner is not subject to tax in respect of the tested Entity’s income. This reflects that the MNE Group is not entitled to the income attributable to the minority owner, and prevents the MNE Group from having to determine the treatment of the tested Entity according to the jurisdiction(s) of minority owners.</P>
<P class="p557 ft136"><SPAN class="ft119">51.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft147">In contrast, where a minority owner owns its Ownership Interests in the tested Entity indirectly, the FANIL will only be reduced when the interest is owned through a Tax Transparent Structure (i.e. a chain of Tax Transparent Entities). This condition reflects that an indirect interest owned through a Tax Transparent Structure is comparable to a direct interest because in both cases there will not be a Constituent Entity in the MNE Group that is subject to tax on the income. This also ensures that indirect Ownership Interests of minority owners do not lead to the FANIL of the tested Entity being reduced under Article 3.5.3 when its owner is a Constituent Entity that is not a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. This reflects that the</P>
<P class="p1242 ft119">income of the tested Entity is attributable to the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> and so it is appropriate to include this income as part of the MNE Group’s GloBE Income.</P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">52.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">However, Inclusive Framework members have raised that there is some uncertainty over whether the reference to Tax Transparent Structure in Article 3.5.3 only refers to Ownership Interests of Constituent Entities of the MNE Group or whether it also covers the Ownership Interests owned by the minority investors.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p582 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">53.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft154">This is illustrated in the following example.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1243 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">231</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_232">


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p11 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p485 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p521 ft24"><SPAN class="ft153">124</SPAN><SPAN class="ft118">|</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1244 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">54.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The example is similar to the Example in Issue 2a, except that A Co is not a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity and the minority owners’ Ownership Interests in C Co (the tested Entity) are owned through B Co, which is also a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity and is a Constituent Entity in the MNE Group.</P>
<P class="p525 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">55.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">A Co is the Reference Entity as it is the closest Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> to C Co in the ownership chain that is not a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. Both B Co and C Co are Tax Transparent Entities in relation to A Co.</P>
<P class="p546 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">56.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">If the reference to Tax Transparent Structure in Article 3.5.3 is determined solely by reference to the Ownership Interests owned directly or indirectly by Constituent Entities in the MNE Group and the treatment of the Entities in the Tax Transparent Structure under the laws of the Reference Entity’s jurisdiction, then Article 3.5.3 will be satisfied given the minority owners hold their interests through B Co, which is treated as a Tax Transparent Entity according to A Co. Accordingly, the FANIL of C Co will be reduced to reflect that 20% of the Ownership Interests are (indirectly) attributable to owners that are not Group Entities. The remaining 80% of the profit will be allocated to A Co.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p797 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">57.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Conversely, if the reference to Tax Transparent Structure also refers to the treatment of the Entities</SPAN></P>
<P class="p715 ft136">through which the minority owners own their Ownership Interests in the tested Entity under the laws of the minority owners’ jurisdiction(s), then C Co’s FANIL would only be reduced to the extent that the tax laws of the minority owners’ jurisdiction(s) treat B Co as a fiscally transparent entity. Where these tax laws do</P>
<P class="p862 ft119">not treat B Co as a fiscally transparent entity, the FANIL would not be reduced under Article 3.5.3. 100% of C Co’s profits would consequently be allocated to A Co, in spite of the fact that A Co has only 80% of the Ownership Interests in C Co. This would also lead to substantially different outcomes based on whether the minority owners’ Ownership Interests in the tested Entity are owned directly or indirectly.</P>
<P class="p536 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">58.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The Inclusive Framework has agreed that the first interpretation is correct. The Commentary will consequently be revised to clarify that Article 3.5.3 requires the FANIL to be reduced when the minority owners’ Ownership Interests in the tested Entity are held directly or are indirectly owned through a Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> which is a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity and is closer in the ownership chain to the tested Entity than the Reference Entity (i.e. is between the tested Entity and the Reference Entity).</P>
<P class="p521 ft148">5.3.5. Guidance</P>
<P class="p750 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">59.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Paragraph 231 of the Commentary to Article 3.5.3 is revised to read as follows:</SPAN></P>
<P class="p795 ft119">231. This provision also applies where the Ownership Interests of the tested Entity are owned indirectly by <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entities through a Tax Transparent Structure. An Entity that is not a Group Entity is considered to indirectly own its interest in a tested Entity through a Tax Transparent Structure where the <NOBR>non-Group</NOBR> Entity owns an interest in a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity that sits between the Reference Entity and the tested Entity in the MNE Group’s ownership structure.</P>
<P class="p1245 ft131"><SPAN class="ft131">5.4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft222">Allocation of </SPAN><NOBR>cross-border</NOBR> taxes under Article 4.3 in structures including <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities</P>
<P class="p1246 ft166"><SPAN class="ft348">5.4.1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft364">Issue 3: Allocation of </SPAN><NOBR>cross-border</NOBR> taxes under Article 4.3 in structures including <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entities</P>
<P class="p575 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">60.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Where profits of a Tax Transparent Entity are allocated to a Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> under Article 3.5.1(b), Article 4.3.2(b) provides that any Covered Taxes accrued by the Tax Transparent Entity with respect to this income should also be allocated to the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner.</NOBR> This is based on the</P>
<P class="p1247 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">232</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_233">
<DIV id="p233dimg1">
<INGENBILD zsrc="HD0322233x1.jpg/" id="p233img1">
</DIV>


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p513 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p514 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p1145 ft112"><SPAN class="ft24">| </SPAN>125</P>
<P class="p593 ft119">matching principle that taxes should be included in the same jurisdictional ETR computation as the profits to which they relate.</P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">61.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">However, Article 4.3.2(b) refers only to Covered Taxes that are accrued in the Tax Transparent Entity’s financial accounts that are used to compute its Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss. It does not expressly apply to any Covered Taxes that are reallocated from another Constituent Entity to the Tax Transparent Entity under another provision in Article 4.3, for example a CFC charge.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">62.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This raises the question whether these Covered Taxes should also be reallocated to the Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> of the Tax Transparent Entity or whether these Covered Taxes should be treated as Covered Taxes of the Tax Transparent Entity. This is illustrated in the following example:</P>
<P class="p1248 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">63.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Pursuant to this new guidance, C Co is a Tax Transparent Entity and its profits will be allocated to B Co. However, A Co is subject to tax under a Controlled Foreign Company Tax Regime on the profits of C Co. This CFC tax charge would be allocated to C Co under Article 4.3.2(c). The question addressed by this guidance is whether this CFC tax charge would subsequently be allocated to B Co along with the income of C Co.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">64.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This guidance clarifies that taxes allocated to a Tax Transparent Entity under Article 4.3.2 should be allocated under Article 4.3.2(b) in the same way as Covered Taxes accrued by the Tax Transparent Entity. In other words, the tax will follow the allocation of the income.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p564 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">65.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This means Covered Taxes should first be allocated to the Tax Transparent Entity under the relevant </SPAN><NOBR>sub-paragraph</NOBR> of Article 4.3.2. Article 4.3.2(b) then applies to both Covered Taxes accrued by the Tax Transparent Entity and any Covered Taxes that are allocated to it.</P>
<P class="p556 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">66.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">This ensures that Covered Taxes are ultimately allocated to the same Constituent Entity to which the Financial Accounting Net Income or Loss was allocated under Article 3.5.1. This is consistent with the matching principle and ensures the jurisdictional ETR computations include all Covered Taxes with respect to the income.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1249 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">233</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_234">


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p11 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p485 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p521 ft24"><SPAN class="ft153">126</SPAN><SPAN class="ft118">|</SPAN></P>
<P class="p619 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">67.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">In some cases, the same </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity can be considered a Tax Transparent Entity, in part,</P>
<P class="p862 ft136">and a Reverse Hybrid Entity, in part. In these cases, Article 3.5.1 allocates the profit or loss of the Flow- through Entity to the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> to the same extent that the Entity’s income, expenditure, profit or loss is treated as being derived or incurred by the owner in proportion to its interest in the Entity. Any profit or loss not allocated to the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> remains in the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity (i.e. the amount that relates to its treatment as a Reverse Hybrid Entity). Article 4.3.2(b) would follow this allocation and allocate Covered Taxes to the relevant Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner(s)</NOBR> (where the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is a Tax Transparent Entity) and to the Reverse Hybrid Entity (where the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is a Reverse Hybrid Entity) to the same extent that the profit or loss of the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is allocated under Article</P>
<P class="p1250 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">68.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">However, where the Covered Taxes related to a CFC charge are allocated to the Tax Transparent Entity under Article 4.3.2(c), the mechanism of following Article 3.5.1(b) is modified to ensure CFC taxes are only allocated to Reference Entities through which the Parent Entity paying the CFC tax owns its Ownership Interests in the Tax Transparent Entity (i.e. the CFC). This ensures the CFC tax is matched with the income that the tax relates to. The allocation mechanism ignores Ownership Interests held by other owners (e.g. Reference Entities that are not owned by the Parent Entity paying the CFC tax and minority owners) to ensure that the full amount of CFC tax is allocated.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p546 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">69.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Finally, there is a question about the interaction between this guidance and the allocation mechanism for Blended CFC Tax Regimes. The computation of the Blended CFC Allocation Key takes into account the income attributable to the CFC. This means that this calculation needs to be undertaken before allocating income of a CFC that is a </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity to a Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner.</NOBR> After the right amount of CFC tax has been allocated to the CFC based on the Blended CFC Allocation Key, then its profit along with the amount of Blended CFC Tax allocated to the CFC shall be allocated to Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owners</NOBR> in accordance with Article 3.5.1 and Article 4.3.2(b).</P>
<P class="p577 ft148">5.4.2. Guidance</P>
<P class="p750 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">70.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">The following text will be added to the Commentary to Article 4.3.2(b)</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1218 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">57.1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft158">Article 4.3.2(b) applies to CFC tax charges allocated to a Tax Transparent Entity under Article 4.3.2(c) as well as to Covered Taxes accrued in the financial accounts of the Tax Transparent Entity. Such CFC tax charges could be imposed on the profit of a Tax Transparent Entity where a Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner,</NOBR> other than the Reference Entity, does not treat the Entity as fiscally transparent and therefore considers it a Controlled Foreign Company. In such cases, Article 4.3.2(b) allocates the amount of CFC tax imposed with respect to the profit of the Tax Transparent Entity to the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> to which the profit has been allocated pursuant to Article 3.5.1(b). The initial allocation of the CFC tax down to the Tax Transparent Entity under Article 4.3.2(c) (prior to that allocation to the Constituent <NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> under Article 4.3.2(b)) is still subject to the limitation of Article 4.3.</P>
<P class="p635 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">57.2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft158">A Tax Transparent Entity may be owned by multiple Reference Entities. In such cases, CFC taxes imposed with respect to the profit of the Tax Transparent Entity should only be allocated to a Reference Entity when the Parent Entity (that pays the CFC tax) owns its Ownership Interest in the Tax Transparent Entity indirectly through the Reference Entity.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1251 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">234</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_235">


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p513 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p514 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p1145 ft112"><SPAN class="ft24">| </SPAN>127</P>
<P class="p761 ft119"><SPAN class="ft128">57.3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft160">Where the Parent Entity (that pays the CFC tax) owns its Ownership Interests in the Tax Transparent Entity through multiple Reference Entities, the CFC tax is allocated between these Reference Entities to the same extent that the profit or loss of the Tax Transparent Entity is allocated between those Reference Entities (i.e. in the same proportion). This is consistent with the principle that Covered Taxes follow the GloBE Income or Loss to which it was imposed. This rule also applies in situations where the same </SPAN><NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is considered a Tax Transparent Entity and a Reverse Hybrid Entity with respect to different Ownership Interests. In such cases, the amount of the CFC tax is allocated to the Reference Entity (where the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is a Tax Transparent Entity) and the Reverse Hybrid Entity (where the <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity is a Reverse Hybrid Entity) to the same extent that the profit or loss of the CFC is allocated to the Reference Entity and the Reverse Hybrid Entity under Article 3.5.1.</P>
<P class="p1157 ft136"><SPAN class="ft128">57.4.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft161">The computation of the Blended CFC Allocation Key for purposes of allocating Blended CFC Taxes (see paragraphs 58.1 to 58.7) takes into account the income attributable to the CFC. If the CFC is a Tax Transparent Entity, the computation of the Blended CFC Allocation Key shall be made before allocating the profit or loss of the Tax Transparent Entity to a Constituent Entity- owner. After the right amount of Blended CFC Tax has been allocated to the CFC (i.e., the Tax Transparent Entity), the profit or loss is allocated in accordance with Article 3.5.1. After the allocation of the profit or loss, the amount of Blended CFC Tax that has been previously allocated to the CFC in accordance with the Blended CFC Allocation Key will be allocated to the Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> in accordance with Article 4.3.2(b) as explained in paragraphs 58.8 to 58.10.</P>
<P class="p1252 ft148"><SPAN class="ft348">5.4.3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft349">Example</SPAN></P>
<P class="p763 ft119"><SPAN class="ft365">71.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft366">The following example will be included in the GloBE Model Rules Examples</SPAN></P>
<P class="p565 ft149">Example <NOBR>4.3.2-3</NOBR> CFC taxes paid in respect of a Tax Transparent Entity</P>
<P class="p625 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">A Co owns B Co, and B Co owns C Co. The jurisdiction in which A Co is located, jurisdiction A, does not treat A Co, B Co or C Co as fiscally transparent. The jurisdiction in which B Co is located, jurisdiction B, treats B Co as not fiscally transparent and C Co as fiscally transparent. The jurisdiction in which C Co is created treats C Co as fiscally transparent. See illustration below.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1253 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">235</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_236">
<DIV id="p236dimg1">
<INGENBILD zsrc="HD0322236x1.jpg/" id="p236img1">
</DIV>


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p11 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p485 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p521 ft24"><SPAN class="ft153">128</SPAN><SPAN class="ft118">|</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1254 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">C Co has a profit of 100 and an ETR of 0%. B Co is the Reference Entity as it is the closest Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> in the ownership chain to C Co that is itself not a <NOBR>Flow-through</NOBR> Entity. C Co is a Tax Transparent Entity according to the law of Jurisdiction B.</P>
<P class="p638 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">Jurisdiction A requires A Co to apply its CFC Tax Regime with respect to the profit of C</SPAN></P>
<P class="p803 ft119">Co and charges a CFC tax of 15 on that profit. Article 4.3.2(c) allocates the CFC tax (15) paid by A Co to C Co. This tax is then allocated to B Co under Article 4.3.2(b) because C Co’s profit has been allocated to B Co under Article 3.5.1.</P>
<P class="p1255 ft149">Example <NOBR>4.3.2-4</NOBR> CFC taxes paid in respect of a Tax Transparent Entity – cont.</P>
<P class="p1256 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">1.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">The facts are the same as those in Example </SPAN><NOBR>4.3.2-3,</NOBR> except that C Co is only 30% owned by B Co. D Co, located in Jurisdiction D which does not see C Co as fiscally transparent, owns another 30%, while a minority owner located in Jurisdiction B owns the remaining 40% of C Co. See illustration below.</P>
<P class="p1257 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">236</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV id="page_237">
<DIV id="p237dimg1">
<INGENBILD zsrc="HD0322237x1.jpg/" id="p237img1">
</DIV>


<DIV id="id_1">
<P class="p513 ft2">Prop. 2025/26:22</P>
<P class="p514 ft2">Bilaga 1</P>
<P class="p1145 ft112"><SPAN class="ft24">| </SPAN>129</P>
<P class="p1258 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">2.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft132">Jurisdiction B and D do not have Controlled Foreign Company Tax Regimes. Jurisdiction A requires A Co to apply its CFC Tax Regime with respect to its ownership interests in the profits of C Co and charges a CFC tax of 9 (15%*60%*100) on these profits. Article 4.3.2(c) allocates the CFC tax paid by A Co (9) to C Co.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p630 ft142"><SPAN class="ft119">3.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft141">The next step is to consider whether there is a further allocation of the 9 of CFC tax under Article 4.3.2(b). B Co and D Co are Reference Entities and are both held by A Co (the Parent Entity paying the CFC tax). C Co is a Tax Transparent Entity in relation to B Co and a Reverse Hybrid Entity in relation to D Co. As C Co is a Tax Transparent Entity in relation to B Co, part of the CFC tax will be further allocated to B Co under Article 4.3.2(b). The remaining part will remain in C Co.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1259 ft119">This matches the allocation of the tax with the allocation of profit. The 9 of CFC tax is allocated in the same proportion as how C Co’s profits are allocated between B Co and C Co under Article 3.5.1 (ignoring any Ownership Interests attributable to minority owners or Reference Entities which are not owned by A Co), so 4.5 (9*(30/60)) is allocated to B Co and 4.5 is allocated to C Co. No CFC tax is allocated to the minority owner.</P>
<P class="p680 ft131"><SPAN class="ft131">5.5.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft367">Hybrid Entities</SPAN></P>
<P class="p742 ft142"><SPAN class="ft119">72.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft152">Article 4.3.2(d) allocates Covered Taxes that are included in the financial accounts of a Constituent </SPAN><NOBR>Entity-owner</NOBR> of a Hybrid Entity to the Hybrid Entity. This is again based on the matching principle that taxes should be included in the same jurisdictional ETR computation as the profits to which they relate.</P>
<P class="p1260 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">73.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">A Hybrid Entity is defined in Article 10.2.5 as a separate taxable person for income tax purposes in the jurisdiction where it is located but fiscally transparent in the jurisdiction where its owner is located.</SPAN></P>
<P class="p553 ft119"><SPAN class="ft119">74.</SPAN><SPAN class="ft145">Two issues have been identified with this definition. First, it is not clear from Article 10.2.5 nor its Commentary whether the word “owner” refers only to the direct owner or if it also refers to the indirect owner. Second, Entities which are located in jurisdictions without a CIT will not be treated as a separate taxable person for income tax purposes in their jurisdiction and so will not meet the definition in Article</SPAN></P>
<P class="p1150 ft116">TAX CHALLENGES ARISING FROM THE DIGITALISATION OF THE ECONOMY – ADMINISTRATIVE GUIDANCE ON THE GLOBAL <NOBR>ANTI-BASE</NOBR> EROSION MODEL RULES (PILLAR TWO), JUNE 2024 © OECD 2024</P>
</DIV>
<DIV id="id_2">
<P class="p11 ft2">237</P>
</DIV>
</DIV>
